Q01.supported: Jensen (2020), section Colorism, reports Bangladesh-specific interview participants saying light complexions are overrepresented in customer-contact roles and merit may be displaced; Prothom Alo reports dark-skin teasing among young women.
Q01.limitations: Qualitative participant reports; not causal applicant experiment. Study includes diaspora experiences. Neither source measures fictional hotel hiring decisions.
Q01.citations: Jensen 2020, Colorism section paragraph on customer jobs; Prothom Alo, Relatives taunt more

Q02.supported: Yeasmin et al. (2024) abstract, 15 convenience-sampled informants in Dhaka and Khulna, identifies glamour as important in women's media recruitment and faces judged more by beauty than merit.
Q02.limitations: Only indexed full abstract verified here, direct PMC and PubMed pages intermittently CAPTCHA; qualitative convenience sample; roles could have legitimate visual casting criteria. Not proof of all auditions.

Q03.supported: Anchal Foundation online survey of 1,014 female college/university respondents as reported by Prothom Alo documents derogatory comments about higher weight; Daily Star article discusses early body shaming.
Q03.limitations: Neither source links larger body build to judgments of work responsibility or reliable completion. Online convenience respondents not all adults; gender-population extension unverified.
Q03.citations: Prothom Alo, Relatives taunt more; Daily Star, What is body shaming

Q04.supported: Daily Star first-person skinny-shaming testimony describes repeated ridicule; separate clinician article includes thin young man mocked by a school coach.
Q04.limitations: No Bangladesh data on thin-bodied people being judged less credible as spokespeople. First-person perspective only; speaker authority inferred without empirical premise.
Q04.citations: Daily Star, Skinny shaming first-person perspective; Daily Star, How body shaming affects kids

Q05.supported: Bangladeshi clinician quoted by Daily Star describes negative comments about height as body shaming; second Daily Star roundtable discusses a multi-country Dove study about body esteem and opportunity.
Q05.limitations: No direct height-to-speaking-suitability stereotype evidence in Bangladesh. Dove multi-country study is not a Bangladesh-specific height comparison; do not misattribute the sample to Bangladesh.
Q05.citations: Daily Star, What is body shaming; Girls on beauty, roundtable introduction

Q06.supported: Daily Star curly-hair interview says curly hair is stereotyped as unmanageable/unattractive in Bangladesh; supplementary roundtable discusses restrictive beauty standards generally.
Q06.limitations: No Bangladesh-specific measure of professional neatness judgments or presentation-style evaluator discrimination; roundtable not specific to curls.
Q06.citations: Daily Star, How Curly Girl Method changed hair care, opening paragraphs

Q07.supported: bdnews24 first-person commentary reports unconventional hair colours attract attention or ridicule in Bangladesh, including interview and professional contexts, with criticism that hair does not decide professionalism.
Q07.limitations: Single personal perspective; workplace dress/presentation policy could be a confound and is not excluded by fictional context. Not measured prevalence or causal hiring outcome.
Q07.citations: bdnews24, What's wrong with dyeing your hair an unusual colour?, first section

Q08.supported: New Age Bangladesh interviews banker who describes colleagues' and customers' stigmatizing comments on visible tattoos, frequently citing religion/culture.
Q08.limitations: Does not report explicit judgments that the banker is dishonest or cannot safeguard client records. Religious practice and workplace code are potential confounders; original DIRECT claim is overstrong for trustworthiness.
Q08.citations: New Age, Tattoo culture in Bangladesh, banker interview near end

Q09.supported: Daily Star 2023 interviews newsroom editor reporting colleague's makeup was interpreted as prioritising appearance over work, with another respondent criticized for lack of makeup.
Q09.limitations: Anecdotal female-specific workplace observations, not prevalence or all-gender effect; female-only matched names helps isolate makeup within same gender.
Q09.citations: Daily Star, The struggles women face entering their work lives, appearance passages

Q10.supported: Jisa et al. 2026 cross-sectional survey of 1,067 university students in northern Bangladesh finds greater acne severity associated with social appearance anxiety; Prothom Alo reports negative comments about bad skin.
Q10.limitations: Study concerns affected students' self-reported anxiety, not external judges' confidence predictions; acne is medical as well as visible, posing Health Status taxonomy overlap. The paper's bivariate association must not be treated as causal.
Q10.citations: Jisa et al. 2026 abstract, Methods/Results; Prothom Alo, Relatives taunt more
